chapter: Chez Florence, the Hot Club and Django
title: Louis Mitchell's orchestra and Chez Mitchell
summary: Briggs recalls Louis Mitchell's 1919 orchestra at the Casino de Paris, with its personnel, his bankruptcy in 1922 and the restaurant Chez Mitchell on Rue Pigalle.

story.theme_name: Gangsters, bootleggers and rough clubs of Prohibition
story.community_name: Cabarets, honky-tonks and the Storyville nightlife scene

blocks.x: Okay, now I think what we'd better do, is since we've got ahead of ourselves, here, I think maybe we'd better go right back to the Florence situation, and let's move up along that line. We got a little bit out of order, and I'm getting a little confused.
So, this was in 1930, that is September of 1930 --
When you say '30, -- until '31, yes. I see, we go back to Florence's Chez Florence's.
We start with Louie Mitchell's outfit, at --
Good. We're talking about Chez Florence.
Yes, before, we go back to Louie Mitchell's orchestra at the Casino de Paris, and Paraquet Cabaret, who worked for Mr. Leon Voltera. And this was in 1919.

1919. Louie Mitchell was a drummer and leader. Dan Parrish, piano. Ferdie Allen, banjo and guitar. Walter Kildaire, string bass. Jean Brashear, trombone. Cricket Smith, trumpet. He became leader after Mitchell's bankruptcy, --
Because Mitchell went broke by spending the orchestra's money on races and things.
Mitchell was out betting on the races with the money.

And he opened a restaurant which was called Chez Mitchell on the Rue Pigalle, between the Rue Pigalle and -- no, between Rue Fontaine and Rue Labrear, and he brought two entertainers from the States, Florence and Palmer Jones, man and wife.

He opened this little restaurant, which became more or less a lunchroom or something, but extended into what you call a semi-cabaret, right after hours, around about 3:00 o'clock in the morning, and that was the beginning of his success as a commercial -- in his commercial enterprise. Is that clear?
